fr:mainmatter.html:p: The database engineer is a reader who does not necessarily know any type theory, but is familiar with SQL, Datalog, Conjunctive queries, Egglog, Automerge, and perhaps some of the methods for incrementalizing queries like DBSP.
There are a variety of intended audiences for this manual; a given reader may fall into several of the following categories.
The categorical logician is a reader who is comfortable with modern approaches to the categorical semantics of type theory, such as:

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The categorical logician also has a reasonable grasp of topos theory and 2-category theory.

The type theorist is a reader who is comfortable with traditional type theory rules given in Gentzen’s tree notation and who might also have some experience with normalization by evaluation, but who is not yet familiar with the modern approaches of The categorical logician.

The database engineer is a reader who does not necessarily know any type theory, but is familiar with SQL, Datalog, Conjunctive queries, Egglog, Automerge, and perhaps some of the methods for incrementalizing queries like DBSP.
The developer is someone who is interested in contributing to geolog, or creating a geolog-like system.

The programmer-user is a reader who intends to incorporate geolog into a larger application. The programmer-user should be familiar with the language that they intend to use geolog from (currently, this is only TypeScript), and should be willing to learn a new language. We say “programmer-user” to distinguish this audience from the user of an application that the “programmer-user” creates; this user needs not read this manual.

The programmer-user who also falls into the earlier categories will benefit from a deeper understanding of geolog. However, geolog is also comprehensible in a self-contained way, just as one does not need to understand cartesian closed categories in order to use lambda x: x + 1 in Python, and it is a goal of this manual to present a clear conceptual picture for the non-mathematical programmer-user.
At various points in the manual we clarify which audience a certain section is for; a reader not in that audience may safely skip that section.

fr:title.text: Type theory as a language for anything

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Type theory as a language for anything

fr:mainmatter.html:p: (This is meant for The type theorist, The database engineer, The developer, The programmer-user)

A programmer with a passing familiarity with type theory may have formed some preconceptions about what a type is, and what it means to give an element of that type. For instance, in a language like Haskell or Rust, types are how we put structure on pieces of computer memory, so that we remember that the value at a certain address is a pointer or integer or floating point number. In a proof assistant, types are used as a foundation for mathematics; types play the role of the “sets” that informal mathematicians use.

The truth is that types do not have any intrinsic meaning. Rather, type theory is a convenient tool for working with any collection of things which relate to each other in certain precise, well-structured ways.
In particular, type theory is a tool for working with things defined by universal properties.
In set theory, if A and B are sets then to produce an element of A \times B it suffices to produce an element of A and an element of B, and vice-versa.
In propositional logic, if P and Q are propositions then to produce a proof of P \wedge Q it suffices to produce a proof of P and a proof of Q, and vice-versa.
In a programming language with tuple types, if a and b are types then to produce an element of (a,b) it suffices to produce an element of a and an element of b, and vice-versa.
In number theory, in order to show that k is a divisor of the GCD (greatest common divisor) of m and n, it suffices show that k is a divisor of m and n, and vice versa.
Again in set theory, if U and V are subsets of a larger set X, then to show that x is an element of U \cap V it suffices to show that x is an element of U and an element of V, and vice-versa.
In group theory, in order to produce a homomorphism from G to the product group H_0 \times H_1, it suffices to produce a homomorphism from G to H_0 and from G to H_1, and vice-versa.
This list could consider ad nauseum, but the reader should get the point by now; there's a pattern going on.
The concept of a universal property is formalized in different ways, often using category theory, but we need not bother with formalization at this stage.

The reader may have heard of “the Curry-Howard correspondence”, often informally referred to “propositions as types”. The Curry-Howard correspondence shows how various type formers and logical connectives correspond. With all due respect to Curry-Howard the name “correspondence” is somewhat of a misnomer because it assumes a false equivalence between the two things that are claimed to be in correspondence. In particular, propositional logic is a mathematical domain in which type theory may be applied to form a convenient syntax; it is by no means the only domain.

The reason type theory may be usefully applied to propositional logic because all of the connectives of propositional logic (and, or, not, forall, exists, etc.) satisfy universal properties; this is the same as the reason why type theory may be applied to any other area.

The way that type theory may be applied to a particular area is via the development of a particular type theory. Confusion between type theory as a subject and the concept of a type theory as a mathematical object is an unfortunate side effect of the nomenclature, because “ breaks with the convention that in group theory, we study groups, in field theory we study fields, or in category theory we study categories.

A particular type theory is merely a syntactic formalization of some collection of universal properties, consisting of a collection of rules by which we judge that a certain piece of syntax is well-typed. The beauty of universal properties is that each universal property is quite self-contained, so a type theory may be designed by systematically observing which universal properties the objects of interest support, and then adding the standard type-theoretic rules for those universal properties to one's type theory.

And this is the method that we have followed in order to design the type theory for geolog: observe the universal properties that our domain of interest (relational databases) satisfy, and add rules corresponding to these universal properties. Fortunately, the result of this systematic development seems to produce a language which expresses many of the important database operations.
DBSP is a language for “describing computations over data streams.” It is defined in DBSP: Automatic Incremental View Maintenance for Rich Query Languages, and currently implemented in Feldera.
SQL, or “Structured Query Language”, is a family of languages used to declaratively access relational databases.
